newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MASSACRE OVER, TAKE YOUR VALENTINE'S RAND TO EUROPE.
newsitem.headline: MASSACRE OVER, TAKE YOUR VALENTINE'S RAND TO EUROPE.

text.p: It's very nice to go
travelling this Valentine's Day, with the rand back in the pink
just about everywhere in the world after its Valentine's Day
massacre on foreign exchange markets last year.
A check on overseas rates shows that after a horrible 1996,
continental Europe has been the most forgiving to South Africa's
currency, making the Alpine ski vacation hardly any more
expensive than it was a year ago.
On Valentine's eve 1997 -- a year after speculators drove a
cruel downward spike into the heart of the currency's health
chart -- the unit is at its highest value in a year in Germany,
Switzerland and Japan.
It's at its best for 11 months or so in France, Spain,
Austria, Sweden and the Netherlands, and it's on a 10-month high
against the Italian lire. Maybe get her that Gucci belt.
In the United States, Britain, Hong Kong, Australia and
Canada the rand has also recovered from the dark days of October
and November last year, but it hasn't come as far or as fast.
Against the pound sterling, the South African unit was
trading at about 7.18 on Thursday, its highest in four months
but still well below last year's Valentine's Day value of 5.60.
A year ago on February 14, the U.S. dollar was worth 3.64
rand. Today it costs 4.40, its cheapest price in seven months.
Against the Hong Kong dollar, the rand was notched at 1.76
on Thursday, its best since late July but still a way short of
the 1996 Valentine's Day value of 2.12 -- so, no vest with the
custom-made suit.
A similar recovery pattern appears against the Australian
and Canadian dollars -- the rand is doing much better, but has a
further slope to climb on the graph before it matches its
performance against the continental Europeans.
Below is a table of some major overseas currency values as
they were quoted by Reuters against the rand on Thursday
morning, and as they were on Valentine's Day last year.
Don't look for these rates at your local bank necessarily.
The tourist will always pay a little more.
